1.0.0.en: “1 Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, 2 ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.’” [1-2].

1.0.1.en: And in the Septuagint: “the cry of their wickedness is come up before me.”

1.0.2.en: The call was unique of its kind, for he is the only prophet who was called to serve a Gentile city, not to prophesy its destruction but to call it to repentance, so that the divine wrath might not fall upon it. It was not possible for this prophet or for anyone else to accept such a call, not out of hatred for the Gentiles but out of love for his own people, as we said before, that the salvation of the Gentiles is accomplished with the fall of Israel, and the faith of the world through the unbelief of the old people (Rom 11:11). In any case, since Jonah could not accept the call with his human mind, he fled; but God, who saw the purity of his heart, used even his flight to accomplish His divine purposes toward the Gentiles.

1.0.3.en: In the Septuagint it says: “for the cry of their wickedness is come up before me.” If the holy life shines in its most perfect form in the Lord Christ, who does not cry, nor does anyone hear His voice in the streets (Mt 12:19), then the wicked life carries in the ears of God a cry or clamor that heaven does not accept and that its Creator does not find restful, revealing the loss of inner peace. The wicked Cain killed his brother Abel and kept his mouth silent about the matter, but the marks of his evil were crying out through the shed blood of his brother, as the Lord says: “The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10), and as it was said of the evil of Sodom and Gomorrah: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great” (Gen 18:20).

1.0.4.en: Jonah, whose name means “dove,” was called to preach in Nineveh, the great city, the cry of whose wickedness rose to heaven, as though God wanted to shatter the cries of evil with the meekness of the dove, to heal the inflamed wounds with soft oil, and to quench fire with water!

1.0.5.en: If the world has turned into unceasing clamor and bitter cries of injustice, it is in need of the Church, or of the true believer, who has the dove's eyes (Song 1:15; 4:1). They are the eyes of the Lord Christ, who says: “Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart” (Mt 11:29), the eyes of the Holy Spirit, the true Dove, that by meekness we may inherit the earth (Mt 5:5) on behalf of the Lord Christ, so that it becomes His Kingdom, filled with joy and peace.

1.0.6.en: If the wicked are earth and not heaven because of their love of earthly things and their attachment to temporal things, then, since we carry within us the true Jonah, we win them by the meekness of His Holy Spirit, so that they no longer remain earth but become heaven. As St. John Climacus says: [The Lord finds rest in meek hearts, but the troubled spirit is the seat of Satan. The meek inherit the earth, or rather they rule over it, but those of evil character are driven from their land].

1.0.7.en: If Nineveh, the great city, represents the body, the cries of whose evil desires rise before the Lord, then no one is able to remove these cries from it except our true Jonah, who fills the soul and sanctifies the body as well.

1.1.0.en: “But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” [3].

1.1.1.en: Why did Jonah want to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord instead of going to Nineveh?

1.1.2.en: First: St. Jerome holds that Jonah could not bear to go to Nineveh and have it saved at the expense of his own people Israel, so he disobeyed the Lord not out of hatred in his heart but out of zeal for his people, as though he were imitating the zealous prophet Moses in his saying: “Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” (Ex 32:32). Moses appeared as one who resisted the Lord, yet he obtained God's mercies for his people, and God did not blot out his name from His book. In the same spirit the Apostle Paul says: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: who are Israelites” (Rom 9:3). He desired that he himself be cut off so that his brethren might live in Christ, counting his death a gain; by this love he did not die but deserved the life he desired for them. So Jonah feared that his preaching to the Assyrians, the enemies of Israel, would mean the destruction of Israel itself, and he fled to Tarshish, that is, in the opposite direction. Some think it is Tartessus, in southern Spain near Gibraltar, or Carthage in North Africa.

1.1.3.en: Second: The word “Tarshish,” as St. Jerome sees it, means “sea” or “contemplation in joy.” If the word “Joppa” in Canaanite means “beauty,” then Jonah, instead of setting out by God's commandment to preach salvation to Nineveh, preferred to go down to the beauty of his human thought and human wisdom, that is, to Joppa, to cast himself into Tarshish, that is, into the sea of this world or into joyful contemplations, without true striving and without actually carrying the Cross. This behavior represents the conduct of the man who walks according to his own desire and not according to the Lord's difficult commandment.

1.1.4.en: Third: The prophet Jonah, while knowing that God is “the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land” (Jon 1:9), and even bearing witness to it, rushes to flee from God when he leans on his human thought apart from faith. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Truly he fled from the land, but he did not flee from the wrath of God! He fled from the earth, but he brought storms upon himself in the sea]. It would have been fitting for him rather not to flee from God but to God, for in Him alone the believer finds his peace and safety!

1.2.0.en: 4 But the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken. 5 Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep. 6 So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, “What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.” 7 And they said every one to his fellow, “Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.

1.2.1.en: If Jonah fled to the sea from the Maker of the sea Himself, the Lord therefore summoned him in a new language fitting for him as a fugitive, the language of successive afflictions, for “the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken” [4]. The Lord began to speak to him in the language of the great wind, the mighty tempest and the ship that had lost its balance, things that suit Jonah and reveal what was within him: a wind of violent disobedience, a great tempest of inner turmoil, and the unbalanced ship of his heart.

1.2.2.en: St. Jerome says: [Jonah's flight points to the condition of man in general, for by despising the commandments of the Lord he fled from His face and gave himself over to the world, and the tempest of the world grew fierce upon him until he was about to drown; then he was compelled to contemplate God and to return to the One from whom he had fled... The ship was in danger... and the waves were stirred up by the winds... for when the Lord is not pleased, nothing is safe].

1.2.3.en: The strangers heard the voice of God, though they did not know Him, while the ears of Jonah grew heavy to hear, for it says: “Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep” [4-5]. The mariners were pagans, and their knowledge of God was mixed with much error, and yet when God spoke in the language of hardship and affliction they were filled with fear and did nothing until each one of them cried out to his god; so God, for them, came first and before everything else, although they did not know Him.

1.2.4.en: St. Jerome says: [They thought the ship was too heavy with its natural cargo, and did not realize that the weight was due to the fugitive prophet. The mariners were afraid, and each one cried out to his god, for they were ignorant of the truth, yet they were not ignorant of divine providence. Through their mistaken religion they knew something and perceived some spiritual depth... But as for Israel, neither prosperity nor pain could lead it to the knowledge of God. Therefore Joshua wept much over the people, while the eyes of the people were dry].

1.2.5.en: The pagans were crying out to their gods and throwing their cargo into the sea, each one praying and working as much as he could, but Jonah, though he knew that he was the cause of the calamity, went down into the sides of the ship to sleep a heavy sleep, as though he did not want to see the waves of God's wrath against him, or like one who took a narcotic to flee from his painful reality.

1.2.6.en: If Jonah's sleep represents a kind of slackness, yet at the same time it gave us a good prophetic aspect. On the one hand, he represented humanity at rest in the Lord amid the waves of this troubled world. When Herod was about to bring out the Apostle Peter to kill him (Acts 12:6), Peter was sleeping soundly, bound with two chains between two soldiers in prison and under strict guard. On the other hand, Jonah represented the Lord Christ, who slept on the Cross as in the ship, to raise up the new Eve from His pierced side, enjoying true rest in Him; He also slept on the Cross so as to be buried in the belly of the earth and rise, granting us the power of the Resurrection. As St. Jerome says: [While the others were in danger, he was safe, sleeping and rising. And at his request, and by the mystery of his sufferings, he saved those who awakened him].

1.3.0.en: Let us return to the mariners and their shipmaster, and we find them acting with surpassing wisdom together with gentleness and meekness, for it says: “So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not. And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah” [6-7].

1.3.1.en: The shipmaster was marked by surpassing meekness in his speech to the prophet, who was sleeping soundly at a time when everyone was crying out and praying and throwing the cargo into the sea... He spoke with exceeding gentleness in which he did not wound his feelings, and urged him to pray kindly, something we sometimes do not find in believers, and even in shepherds themselves, who lose their peace when rebuking and lose their calm while setting others right.

1.3.2.en: We say that God, who had earlier spoken with the prophet, perhaps through a vision or a revelation concerning the work in Nineveh, came back to speak to him through raging nature, and since he had stopped his ears, He spoke to him through the pagans, saying to him: “What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.” As though He were saying: “Why are you sleeping inside your heart? Your God from whom you flee is able to save us Gentiles from perishing. If you love your people and your nation, listen to our supplications, look upon our longing, and do not despise our faith. Even if we do not yet know the God whom you worship, by faith we accept Him, so let us not perish!”

1.3.3.en: Remarkably, the sailors cast lots, and God revealed the truth, and they realized that Jonah was the cause of God's wrath... As St. Jerome says: [If God guided them through the lot, He is only speaking to them through their own thinking, and this does not justify our use of lots. God guided Balaam through his ass (Num 22:28), to show him that the dumb beast perceived what man in his wickedness did not perceive, and as God spoke with the Magi through the star, and as He allowed Caiaphas to prophesy without knowing it when he said that one man should die for all the people. In any case, if Jonah in his love for his people made light of the salvation of the Gentiles, God revealed to him through the lot that He does not despise a Gentile, but speaks to them in their own language and reveals the truth to them even through their own practice; so what the lot presented carried a hidden divine rebuke to Jonah, who made light of the salvation of the Gentiles!].

1.4.0.en: 8 Then said they unto him, “Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou?” 9 And he said unto them, “I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.” 10 Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, “Why hast thou done this?” For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them. 11 Then said they unto him, “What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us?” for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous. 12 And he said unto them, “Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.”

1.4.1.en: “Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil is upon us; What is thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what is thy country? and of what people art thou? And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land” [8-9].

1.4.2.en: In the midst of the violent currents, the mighty tempest and the surrounding danger, we would have expected the mariners to lose their peace and calm, but they proved to be wise; since they saw a mystery in Jonah, they began to ask him about his whole life in detail... seeking true knowledge. Their questions were a gentle rebuke that God used to set Jonah himself right, for while they were asking, it was fitting for Jonah to examine himself about his conduct. As St. Jerome said: [The purpose of the lot was that the mariners would press him to confess with his own tongue the cause of this tempest and the reason for God's wrath]. That is, to confess his disobedience to the Lord and his flight from the One who made the sea and the dry land.

1.4.3.en: The questions brought the desired result, for he confessed, saying: “I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.” As St. Jerome says: [He did not say “I am an Hebrew” meaning the title proper to his people, belonging to one of its tribes, but he meant that he is a passer-by like Abraham, as though saying: I am weak and a wayfarer like all my fathers, as it says in the Psalm: “They went from one city to another and from one kingdom to another people...” I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, and not the gods to whom you pray, which are unable to save. I pray to the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land, the sea to which I flee, and the land from which I flee!].

1.5.0.en: Jonah confessed his fault, and the mariners came to know the truly fearful God, for it says: “Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them” [10]. They understood that he was a holy man fleeing from the holy God, so they asked him not to rebuke him but, as St. Jerome says: [inquiring about the mystery of his conduct].

1.6.0.en: After enjoying the knowledge of God they asked Jonah: “What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous” [11].

1.6.1.en: St. Jerome says: [As though they were saying: You say that because of you the wind, the waves and the sea are in turmoil. You have revealed to us the cause of the sickness, so disclose the remedy. Behold, the sea rises against us, and we know that we have become the object of wrath because we took you. We erred in receiving you as a guest, so what shall we do that the wrath of God may be calmed toward us? What shall we do to you? Shall we kill you? But you are of those who believe in the Lord! Shall we keep you? You are fleeing from God! Now we have nothing but to carry out your command, so command us, that the sea may be calm, for its turmoil bears witness to the wrath of the Creator... There can be no more delay before the vengeance of the Creator?].

1.7.0.en: “And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you” [12].

1.7.1.en: Jonah offered the remedy, which was to cast him into the raging sea so that the great tempest might be calm, for the tempest was because of his disobedience to the Lord and would not calm except by throwing him into the waters for his repentance; and on the other hand, Jonah, as a representative of the Lord Christ, who bore the sins of the world, had to be cast upon the Cross and delivered to the tomb, that the believers in Him might enjoy reconciliation with the Father and enter into His eternal peace.

1.7.2.en: St. John Chrysostom says: [Jonah expected to flee by means of the ship, but the ship became chains to him]. He thought he could flee from the God of the sea by means of a ship, but God seized him amid the raging waters inside the ship, to confine him in distress and bring him to repentance. God used the very means that Jonah thought was his escape from the hand of God in order to seize him and bring him back to Himself. How beautiful is the statement of St. John Chrysostom: [There was no need for many days or for continual counsels, but simply put, there was need that everything lead him to repentance (that is, God uses all circumstances for his salvation). For God did not lead him from the ship directly to the city, but the mariners handed him over to the sea, and the sea to the whale, and the whale to God, and God to the people of Nineveh, and through this long circuit He brought back the wanderer, so that all might know that it is not possible to flee from the hand of God].

1.7.3.en: St. Jerome comments on the words Jonah spoke to the mariners, saying: [This tempest is seeking me; it threatens you with drowning so that you may seize me, and by my death you will live! I know in truth that this great tempest is because of me... Behold, the waves command you to cast me into the sea, and you will find calm... Let us notice here the greatness of the fugitive: he does not evade, nor conceal the matter, nor deny it after confessing his flight from God, but accepts the punishment with a wide heart. He wants to die so that others may not be destroyed because of him].

1.7.4.en: St. Jerome also has a beautiful comment on these words of Jonah as a prophecy about the work of the Lord Christ, our true Jonah, who accepted to die to redeem all the people, saying: [Our Jonah says: I know in truth that for my sake this great tempest is upon you; for since the winds see me sailing with you to Tarshish, that is, to “joyful contemplation,” I lead you to glory, so that where I am, there you may be also with the Father; therefore wrath occurs. The world weeps and nature is troubled! Death wants to swallow me so as to kill you at the same time, not realizing that it takes me as bait, for by my death it dies! Take me, then, and cast me into the sea!]

1.8.s.en: 5. Jonah in the belly of the fish:

1.8.0.en: 13 Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. 14 Wherefore they cried unto the LORD, and said, “We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O LORD, hast done as it pleased thee.” 15 So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging. 16 Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the LORD, and made vows. 17 Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

1.8.1.en: “Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring it to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. Wherefore they cried unto the LORD, and said, We beseech thee, O LORD, we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, O LORD, hast done as it pleased thee” [13-14].

1.8.2.en: This book brings out in simplicity the good aspects of these Gentiles. At the beginning they did not throw their cargo overboard, nor act according to their experience as sailors, until each one had cried out to his god; so they put their gods first, before their experience, something many believers ignore. Again, when they cast lots and the lot fell on Jonah, they did not wound his feelings with a word nor insult him, despite the many losses that came upon them because of him; and even when he confessed his fault and pointed them to throw him into the sea, they tried to save him by every means, and when they failed completely and realized that it was God's will that they cast him into the sea, they were trembling, fearing the wrath of God, and asking Him not to let them perish for the life of this man! Were not these actions, full of love, gentleness and wisdom, enough to rebuke Jonah, whom the Lord called for the salvation of the Gentiles in Nineveh, yet he fled! It presented to him a sample of Gentiles who surpass the believers themselves. If they were compared with the Jews, who had the Law and the prophecies with them and saw the wonderful works of Christ and the witness of heaven and earth and the sea and all His creation; even Pilate the Gentile washed his hands before them, and yet they cried “His blood be on us, and on our children,” are they not counted better than they?!

1.8.3.en: St. Jerome comments on the actions of the mariners, saying:

1.8.4.en: [They wanted to draw the oar and defeat nature so as not to disgrace the prophet of the Lord... They thought they were able to save the ship from danger, and did not take into account the role Jonah had to play, that he must suffer].

1.8.5.en: [Great was the faith of the mariners, for they were in danger and yet were praying for the life of another. They knew well that spiritual death is more dreadful than natural death, for they said: “lay not upon us innocent blood.” They make God Himself a witness, so that He would not accuse them of what they could not prevent, as though they were saying to Him: We do not want to kill Your prophet; rather he declared Your wrath against him, and the tempest confirmed Your will, O Lord, which we are carrying out with our hands].

1.8.6.en: [While the Gentiles did not want the death of Christ, affirming that it was innocent blood (Mt 27:25), the Jews say: “His blood be on us, and on our children”; therefore when they lift their hands toward heaven they are not answered, because their hands are full of blood].

1.9.0.en: “So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging” [15].

1.9.1.en: St. Jerome says: [It does not say “they seized him” or “they fell upon him,” but “they took him up,” as those who carried him with respect and honor, and cast him into the sea, he having given himself into their hands without resistance; then the sea ceased from its raging, for it found the one it was seeking. When we follow the trail of a fugitive we run after him with all the power of our feet, and when we seize him we stop with the prize. So the sea was raging without Jonah, and when the one it desired was taken into its depths, it rejoiced at taking him, kept festival for him, and grew calm with joy].

1.9.2.en: St. John Chrysostom sees in the casting of the disobedient Jonah into the sea an indication of the expulsion of sin from the ship of our life, that our true peace, which our iniquities took away, may return to us, for he says: [The city was troubled because of the sins of the people of Nineveh, and the ship was troubled because of the prophet's disobedience. Therefore the mariners cast Jonah into the deep, and the ship was preserved. Let us also cast out our sins, and our city will remain in sure safety!].

1.9.3.en: St. Jerome sees in the casting of Jonah into the sea an indication of the sufferings of the Lord Christ, which removed the raging of our sea and saved the ship and those in it from danger. Through the sufferings of the Lord Christ the world was filled with surpassing inner peace!

1.10.0.en: “Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the LORD, and made vows” [16].

1.10.1.en: When Jonah was cast into the sea, that is, when the Lord Christ bore sufferings unto death, He saved us from the old pagan worship, granting us His great fear, the offering of His unique propitiatory sacrifice, and the fulfillment of our vows to the Lord, that is, the complete consecration of our life to Him.

1.10.2.en: St. Jerome says: [When the fugitive Jonah died in the sea, the ship that was shaken by the winds was saved, and the idolaters were saved]. He also says: [Before the sufferings of the Lord they prayed to their gods under the influence of fear (Jon 1:10), but after the sufferings they feared Him, that is, they worshiped and glorified Him... They feared Him exceedingly, that is, with all the soul and all the heart and all the mind (Deut 6:5; Mt 22:37). And they offered a sacrifice; certainly this does not mean the literal sense, for there are no sacrifices in the sea, but the sacrifice of the Lord is the genuine spirit, as it is said: “Offer unto the Lord the sacrifice of praise; and pay thy vows unto the most High” (Ps 49:14)]...

1.10.3.en: Therefore by the casting of Jonah into the sea, or the Lord Christ's entering into His sufferings, the spirit of the fear of God came upon us, and we gained the right to offer His holy sacrifice and to fulfill our vows to Him!

1.10.4.en: “Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights” [7].

1.10.5.en: Things did not proceed without divine ordering or planning, but God, who sent the great wind so that a mighty tempest arose declaring God's wrath against disobedience, is the One who sent a huge fish beside the ship to swallow Jonah, to give him a safe lodging and not death, revealing to him God's care for him. St. Jerome says: [The Lord showed His wrath when Jonah was in the ship, and showed His joy when he entered into death], explaining that this is because he represents the Lord Christ, who put death to death by His death. Truly Jonah appeared as a victim of death swallowed by hell, but it could not hold him within more than three days and three nights, but cast him out of its belly, so that the prophet might say: “O death, where are thy plagues? O Hades, where is thy sting?” (Hos 13:14).

1.10.6.en: The Lord Christ affirmed what happened to Jonah in the belly of the fish as a type of what happened to the Lord Himself, by saying: “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Mt 12:40).

1.10.7.en: How did the Lord Christ remain in the earth for this period?

1.10.8.en: First: St. Jerome holds that the Jews count part of a day as a whole day, so the period of the Lord Christ's death is counted from Friday to Sunday, although He died at the end of Friday and rose at dawn on Sunday. St. John Chrysostom holds that if the Lord had remained until the end of Sunday, the soldiers would have left the tomb, and the Jews would have believed that the news of the Resurrection was the work of the disciples, fabricated after the soldiers left the site; therefore He rose while the soldiers were guarding the tomb.

1.10.9.en: Second: St. Jerome presents an opinion held by some, which is to consider the hours of darkness on the Cross as a new night, unique of its kind.

1.10.10.en: Third: Some count the period of burial from the moment the Lord delivered His broken Body into the bowels of His disciples at the Last Supper, as one buried in the human earth to raise it with Him as a heaven for Himself by His Resurrection at dawn on Sunday.

1.10.11.en: In any case, the Lord was buried three days and rose; this is the truth to which the disciples bore witness and which the Lord confirmed with many proofs, that we might live it as the mystery of our daily resurrection and our victory over death and hell.

1.10.12.en: Moreover, Jonah, by his entering into death and coming out, was used as a living proof of the resurrection of the body on the last day.
